resources.label: Microsoft Learn: Explore core data concepts
Microsoft Learn: Explore relational data in Azure
Microsoft Learn: Explore non-relational data in Azure
Microsoft Learn: Explore data analytics in Azure

flashcards.back: Structured data fits a fixed schema of rows and columns, like a relational table. Semi-structured data has some organization, like tags or key-value pairs, but no fixed schema, like JSON or XML. Unstructured data has no predefined organization at all, like images, video, or free-form text.
flashcards.detail: The exam tests whether you can classify a described dataset into one of these three buckets — JSON and XML are the classic semi-structured examples to remember.

flashcards.back: A workload optimized for many short, fast read/write transactions, like inserting an order or updating a customer record — the backbone of day-to-day operational applications.
flashcards.detail: Think of OLTP as the system running the business minute to minute: e-commerce checkouts, ATM withdrawals, booking systems.

flashcards.back: A workload optimized for complex analytical queries over large volumes of historical data, aggregating and summarizing for reporting and business intelligence rather than fast single-record transactions.
flashcards.detail: OLAP is the analytics side: think data warehouses and Power BI reports built on years of aggregated sales data, not a single order lookup.

flashcards.back: Relational databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and relationships enforced through keys, queried with SQL. Non-relational (NoSQL) databases store data in flexible formats, like documents, key-value pairs, or graphs, built for scale and schema flexibility over strict structure.
flashcards.detail: Neither type is universally the better choice — the exam wants you to match the data shape and consistency needs of a scenario to the right category.

flashcards.back: CSV: plain-text, row-based, human readable. JSON: semi-structured, key-value, widely used for APIs. Parquet and ORC: columnar binary formats optimized for compression and analytics. Avro: row-based binary format popular for streaming data with an embedded schema.
flashcards.detail: Columnar formats like Parquet are the answer whenever a scenario stresses fast analytical queries over just a few columns of a huge dataset.

flashcards.back: A Database Administrator (DBA) provisions, secures, monitors, and maintains databases. A Data Engineer designs and builds data pipelines and storage systems that move and transform data. A Data Analyst explores data and builds reports and visualizations to support business decisions.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario is about building an ETL pipeline, that is a Data Engineer; if it is about building a dashboard, that is a Data Analyst; if it is about backups and performance tuning, that is a DBA.

flashcards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees a relational database transaction provides: a transaction either fully completes or fully fails, data stays valid, concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other, and committed changes survive a crash.
flashcards.detail: ACID is closely associated with relational, OLTP-style databases; many NoSQL stores trade some of these guarantees for scale and flexibility.

flashcards.front: The four V's of big data
flashcards.back: Volume (amount of data), Velocity (speed data arrives and must be processed), Variety (different data types and formats), and Veracity (trustworthiness and quality of the data) — the characteristics commonly used to describe big data workloads.
flashcards.detail: A scenario mentioning huge volumes arriving continuously from many different source formats, some of uncertain quality, is describing all four V's at once.

flashcards.front: Database vs. data warehouse vs. data lake
flashcards.back: A database stores day-to-day operational data. A data warehouse stores large volumes of structured, cleaned, historical data organized for reporting and analytics. A data lake stores massive amounts of raw data of any type before it is necessarily processed.
flashcards.detail: A data lake accepts data before it is necessarily structured; a data warehouse expects data to already be modeled and cleaned before it arrives.

flashcards.back: The standard language for defining, querying, and managing data in a relational database, covering data definition (creating tables), data manipulation (inserting, updating, deleting rows), and data queries (retrieving rows with SELECT).
flashcards.detail: DP-900 expects you to recognize SQL's purpose and the general DDL/DML/query distinction conceptually, not to write complex T-SQL yourself.

flashcards.back: A relational database organizes data into tables, where each row represents one record and each column represents one attribute of that record, with every row in a table sharing the same set of columns.
flashcards.detail: This fixed, tabular shape is what separates relational data from the flexible shape of most non-relational data stores.

flashcards.back: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another table, creating a relationship between the two tables.
flashcards.detail: Foreign keys are the mechanism that lets relational databases enforce referential integrity between related tables, like Orders and Customers.

flashcards.back: The process of organizing tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity, typically by splitting data into multiple related tables instead of repeating the same information in one large table.
flashcards.detail: A repeated customer name and address on every single order row is a normalization smell — that data belongs in its own Customers table, referenced by a foreign key.

flashcards.back: A fully managed platform-as-a-service (PaaS) relational database in Azure, based on the Microsoft SQL Server engine, with automatic patching, backups, and high availability handled by Microsoft.
flashcards.detail: This is the go-to answer whenever a scenario wants a modern SQL Server-compatible database with the least possible management overhead.

flashcards.back: A PaaS deployment option offering near-complete compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including features like cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent, making it easier to lift-and-shift an existing SQL Server estate into Azure.
flashcards.detail: Choose Managed Instance over Azure SQL Database when an existing on-premises workload depends on instance-level features that Azure SQL Database does not support.

flashcards.front: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
flashcards.back: An infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) option that runs full SQL Server inside a customer-managed Azure VM, giving complete control over the OS and SQL Server configuration, at the cost of the customer handling OS patching themselves.
flashcards.detail: This is the right answer whenever a scenario needs OS-level access or a SQL Server version or feature not available in the PaaS options.

flashcards.front: Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL
flashcards.back: Fully managed PaaS offerings for the open-source PostgreSQL and MySQL database engines, giving the same automatic patching, backup, and scaling benefits as Azure SQL Database, for organizations already standardized on those engines.
flashcards.detail: These exist so teams do not have to migrate off PostgreSQL or MySQL just to get a managed Azure experience.

flashcards.back: The DTU (Database Transaction Unit) model bundles compute, memory, and storage into fixed performance tiers. The vCore model lets you independently choose compute and storage, and can apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to reuse existing SQL Server licenses.
flashcards.detail: vCore is the more flexible, and generally more cost-transparent, of the two — and it is the one that supports bringing your own SQL Server license.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database service, built for low-latency access at massive scale, with turnkey global distribution and multiple consistency level options.
flashcards.detail: Cosmos DB is the flagship non-relational answer on this exam whenever a scenario needs global scale with low latency.

flashcards.back: Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs over the same underlying engine: the NoSQL (Core) API for JSON documents, the API for MongoDB, the API for Cassandra (column-family), the Gremlin API (graph data), and the Table API (key-value).
flashcards.detail: Picking the right API usually comes down to what your application or existing skill set already uses — the MongoDB API for teams already using MongoDB drivers, Gremlin for graph and relationship-heavy data, and so on.

flashcards.back: A NoSQL key-value store for large amounts of structured, non-relational data, where each entity is accessed by a partition key and a row key, ideal for fast lookups of simple data at low cost.
flashcards.detail: Table Storage is a simpler, cheaper alternative to using Cosmos DB's Table API when global distribution or guaranteed low-latency SLAs are not required.

flashcards.back: Object storage for large amounts of unstructured data, like images, video, log files, and backups, organized into containers, with access tiers (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive) to balance storage cost against retrieval speed.
flashcards.detail: Blob Storage is the default answer for storing unstructured files at scale in Azure.

flashcards.back: Fully managed file shares in the cloud, accessible via the standard SMB and NFS protocols, so they can be mounted concurrently by multiple VMs or on-premises machines just like a traditional network file share.
flashcards.detail: Azure Files is the answer whenever a scenario wants a lift-and-shift replacement for an on-premises file server, not just object storage for an application.

flashcards.back: A set of capabilities built on top of Azure Blob Storage that adds a hierarchical namespace (real directories and folders) and fine-grained access control, purpose-built for large-scale big data analytics workloads.
flashcards.detail: Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob Storage plus a hierarchical namespace — not a separate storage product built from scratch.

flashcards.back: A data warehouse stores large volumes of structured, historical data optimized for reporting. A star schema organizes that data into a central fact table (measurable events, like sales) surrounded by dimension tables (descriptive context, like product, customer, or date).
flashcards.detail: Fact tables hold the numbers you aggregate; dimension tables hold the descriptive labels you slice and filter by.

flashcards.back: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before loading it into the destination store. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first and transforms it afterward, taking advantage of the destination's own compute power.
flashcards.detail: Modern cloud-scale analytics, including tools like Azure Synapse and Databricks, increasingly favor ELT because the destination often has more processing power than a separate transform step.

flashcards.back: Batch processing collects and processes data in large groups on a schedule, like a nightly job. Streaming, or real-time, processing processes data continuously as each event arrives, with results available within seconds or less.
flashcards.detail: A scenario asking for second-level insight as events happen is streaming; a scenario processing an entire day's transactions overnight is batch.

flashcards.back: A unified analytics service combining big data and data warehousing, offering serverless and dedicated SQL pools for querying data, along with built-in Apache Spark pools, in a single workspace.
flashcards.detail: Synapse is the answer whenever a scenario wants one platform that spans data warehousing, big data (Spark), and pipeline orchestration together.

flashcards.back: A cloud-based data integration service for building, scheduling, and orchestrating ETL/ELT pipelines that move and transform data between many different source and destination systems.
flashcards.detail: Data Factory is about moving and orchestrating data, not analyzing it directly — think of it as the plumbing that feeds a data warehouse or data lake.

flashcards.back: An Apache Spark-based analytics platform, optimized for large-scale data engineering, data science, and machine learning workloads, offered as a first-party Azure service.
flashcards.detail: Databricks is the go-to answer for big-data processing and machine learning at scale, distinct from Synapse's broader warehouse-plus-everything scope.

flashcards.back: A fully managed real-time analytics service for processing and analyzing streaming data, such as telemetry from IoT devices or clickstream data, as it arrives, using a SQL-like query language.
flashcards.detail: Stream Analytics is the dedicated real-time processing answer, as distinct from Data Factory, which is built for scheduled, batch-style orchestration.

flashcards.back: An end-to-end, software-as-a-service analytics platform that unifies data engineering, data integration, data warehousing, data science, and Power BI on top of a single shared data lake called OneLake.
flashcards.detail: Fabric is the newest, most consolidated answer — think of it as bringing Synapse, Data Factory, and Power BI together under one SaaS umbrella with one copy of the data in OneLake.

flashcards.back: A business intelligence suite for connecting to data sources, modeling data, and building interactive reports and dashboards, made up of Power BI Desktop (authoring), the Power BI Service (publishing and sharing), and Power BI Mobile.
flashcards.detail: Power BI typically sits on top of a data warehouse, data lake, or another data source to turn it into interactive reports and dashboards.

flashcards.front: Import vs. DirectQuery mode in Power BI
flashcards.back: Import mode copies data into Power BI's own fast in-memory model for the best query performance, refreshed periodically on a schedule. DirectQuery leaves the data in its source system and queries it live on each interaction, trading some performance for always-current data.
flashcards.detail: DirectQuery is the right choice when data must always reflect the live source; Import mode is the right choice when speed matters most and slightly stale data is acceptable.

flashcards.back: A separate data structure that lets a database find rows matching a query without scanning every row in a table, at the cost of extra storage and slightly slower writes since the index itself must also be updated.
flashcards.detail: A primary key vs. foreign key column is commonly indexed automatically, since it’s exactly the kind of column queries filter and join on most often.

flashcards.back: An architecture combining a data lake’s low-cost, flexible storage for any file type with a data warehouse’s structured, query-optimized layer on top — one platform for both raw and curated data instead of maintaining two separate systems.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft Fabric is built around exactly this lakehouse pattern, unifying what used to be separate lake and warehouse services described under database vs. data warehouse vs. data lake into one workspace.

flashcards.back: A fact table stores the numeric, measurable events at the center of a star schema — like a sales amount or a quantity sold. Dimension tables store the descriptive context around those facts — product, customer, date — used to filter and group them.
flashcards.detail: This is exactly the split inside Data warehouse and star schema — the fact table is what you aggregate; the dimension tables are what you slice and filter by.

flashcards.front: Serverless SQL pool vs. dedicated SQL pool
flashcards.back: A serverless SQL pool in Azure Synapse Analytics bills per query based on data processed, with no infrastructure to provision ahead of time. A dedicated SQL pool provisions and bills for continuously-running compute, sized in advance for predictable, heavy workloads.
flashcards.detail: Ad hoc, unpredictable exploration favors serverless (pay only when you actually query); a large, steady reporting workload favors dedicated, since its provisioned compute is cheaper per-query at real scale.

flashcards.back: The overall practice of managing data quality, access, ownership, and compliance across an organization — deciding who can see what data, ensuring it stays accurate, and tracking where it came from.
flashcards.detail: Data professional roles like a data steward or data owner exist specifically to carry out data governance responsibilities day to day, rather than governance being an abstract policy with no one actually responsible for it.

questions.question: A retailer stores each customer order as a JSON document with a flexible set of fields that can vary from order to order. How should this data best be classified?
questions.explanation: JSON documents have some organization, like keys and nesting, but no fixed schema shared identically by every record, which is the definition of semi-structured data. Structured and relational data require a fixed schema of rows and columns, and unstructured data, like a plain video file, has no inherent organization at all.

questions.question: An application needs to record thousands of small, fast purchase transactions per second, each affecting only a few rows at a time. Which type of workload is this?
questions.explanation: OLTP workloads are optimized for many fast, small, individual transactions, like recording a single purchase, matching thousands of small operations per second. OLAP and data warehousing are optimized for large analytical queries over historical data rather than fast individual writes, and batch analytics processes data in scheduled groups rather than transaction by transaction.

questions.question: A data engineering team needs to store a huge dataset in a format optimized for fast analytical queries that scan only a few columns at a time, with strong compression. Which file format best fits?
questions.explanation: Parquet is a columnar binary format that lets analytical queries scan only the columns they need with strong compression, making it well suited to large-scale analytics. CSV and plain text logs are row-based and largely uncompressed, and XML is verbose and not optimized for column-level analytical scans.

questions.question: A social media application needs to store rapidly changing, loosely structured user activity data at massive global scale, with flexible schemas that evolve often. Which type of database is generally the better fit?
options: A relational database with a fixed schema
questions.explanation: A non-relational (NoSQL) database is built for flexible, evolving schemas and massive horizontal scale, matching a social app's loosely structured, high-volume activity data. A relational database assumes a fixed schema, and a data warehouse or OLAP cube is built for structured historical reporting, not rapidly changing operational data.

questions.question: Which role is primarily responsible for provisioning, securing, monitoring, and maintaining an organization's databases?
questions.explanation: A Database Administrator provisions, secures, monitors, and maintains databases day to day. A Data Analyst builds reports and visualizations, a Data Scientist builds predictive models, and a Business Analyst focuses on business requirements rather than the database itself.

questions.question: A banking application must guarantee that a funds transfer either fully completes, moving money out of one account and into another, or does not happen at all, even if the system crashes mid-transfer. Which property is this describing?
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees a transaction either fully completes or fully fails as one indivisible unit, which is exactly the all-or-nothing funds transfer being described. Velocity and variety are big data characteristics unrelated to transaction guarantees, and elasticity describes automatic scaling of resources, not transactional integrity.

questions.question: A dataset arrives continuously from thousands of IoT sensors, in several different formats, at high volume, with some readings of uncertain accuracy. Which big data characteristic specifically refers to the uncertain accuracy of the readings?
questions.explanation: Veracity refers specifically to the trustworthiness and accuracy of data, which matches readings of uncertain accuracy. Volume refers to the amount of data, velocity to the speed it arrives, and variety to the different formats involved — none of those describe how trustworthy the data is.

questions.question: A team wants to ingest massive amounts of raw data of every type — video, JSON logs, and CSV extracts — without first defining a fixed schema, to be processed and structured later. Which storage concept fits best?
questions.explanation: A data lake is built to accept massive amounts of raw data of any type, structured or not, without requiring a schema up front. A relational database and a data warehouse both expect data to already be structured and modeled, and an OLAP cube is a pre-aggregated structure built on top of already-modeled data, not a raw ingestion target.

questions.question: OLTP workloads are optimized for large, complex analytical queries rather than many fast individual transactions.
questions.explanation: This describes OLAP, not OLTP. OLTP workloads are optimized for many fast, small transactions, like inserting a single order, while OLAP workloads are optimized for complex analytical queries over large volumes of historical data.

questions.question: Semi-structured data, like a JSON document, has some organizational elements such as tags or key-value pairs, but does not require a rigid, fixed schema.
questions.explanation: This is the core distinction between semi-structured and structured data: some organization exists, but it is flexible rather than a strictly fixed schema shared identically by every record.

questions.question: A Data Engineer's primary responsibility is typically building dashboards and visual reports for business stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Building dashboards and reports is typically the responsibility of a Data Analyst. A Data Engineer focuses on designing and building the data pipelines and storage systems that move and transform data.

questions.question: ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) describes a set of properties that guarantee reliable relational database transactions.
questions.explanation: ACID is exactly this set of transaction guarantees, closely associated with relational, OLTP-style databases.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of unstructured or semi-structured data? (Select all that apply)
options: A JSON document with a flexible set of fields
A row in a table with a fixed set of columns
A CSV file where every row shares the same fixed columns
questions.explanation: A JSON document is semi-structured, and a video file is unstructured — neither has a rigid, uniform schema. A table row and a CSV file with fixed shared columns are both structured data, since every record follows the exact same predefined schema.

questions.question: Which of the following are data professional roles commonly referenced in Azure data fundamentals? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Database Administrator, Data Engineer, and Data Analyst are the core data-focused roles covered here. A Network Administrator focuses on network infrastructure, not data storage, pipelines, or analysis.

questions.question: In a relational database table, what uniquely identifies each individual row?
questions.explanation: A primary key is the column, or set of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key instead references a primary key in another table, a partition key is a non-relational storage concept, and an index alone speeds up lookups but does not by itself guarantee uniqueness.

questions.question: A Customers table and an Orders table are related so that every order must reference a valid, existing customer. Which concept enforces this rule?
options: A foreign key referencing the Customers table
A primary key on the Orders table
questions.explanation: A foreign key in the Orders table that references the Customers table's primary key is exactly the mechanism that enforces every order pointing to a valid customer. Normalization is the broader design process, a primary key on Orders only identifies order rows themselves, and a star schema is a data warehouse modeling pattern, not a relational integrity rule.

questions.question: Splitting a single large table that repeats customer address details on every order row into two related tables, Orders and Customers, is an example of which process?
questions.explanation: Splitting repeated data into separate related tables to reduce redundancy is the definition of normalization. Denormalization does the opposite — deliberately reintroducing redundancy for read performance — while sharding and partitioning are about distributing data across physical storage, not about eliminating redundant columns.

questions.question: A company is migrating an on-premises SQL Server database that relies on cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent jobs, and wants the least re-engineering while still moving to a managed Azure service. Which option fits best?
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server compatibility, including cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent, making it the best fit for a lift-and-shift with minimal re-engineering. Azure SQL Database does not support cross-database queries or SQL Agent the same way, and Table Storage and Cosmos DB are non-relational services entirely.

questions.question: A team needs full administrative control over the operating system hosting their SQL Server instance, including installing custom OS-level software alongside it. Which deployment option fits?
options: SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine
questions.explanation: SQL Server on an Azure VM is an IaaS option, giving full administrative control over the operating system, including installing arbitrary OS-level software. Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance are both PaaS, where Microsoft manages the OS, and Azure Database for MySQL is a different database engine entirely.

questions.question: A company already runs its application on open-source PostgreSQL and wants a fully managed Azure equivalent without switching database engines. Which service fits?
questions.explanation: Azure Database for PostgreSQL is the managed PaaS offering for the PostgreSQL engine specifically, letting a team keep using PostgreSQL without switching engines. Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance both run the SQL Server engine, and Cosmos DB is a non-relational database, not a relational PostgreSQL-compatible service.

questions.question: Which purchasing model for Azure SQL Database lets you independently scale compute and storage, and supports applying an existing SQL Server license through Azure Hybrid Benefit?
questions.explanation: The vCore-based purchasing model lets compute and storage scale independently and supports Azure Hybrid Benefit to reuse an existing SQL Server license. The DTU model bundles compute, memory, and storage together into fixed tiers instead, the Basic tier is just one small DTU tier, and the Archive access tier is a Blob Storage concept unrelated to SQL Database purchasing.

questions.question: Normalization organizes relational tables specifically to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.
questions.explanation: That is the definition and purpose of normalization — splitting data into related tables instead of repeating it.

questions.question: Azure SQL Managed Instance offers near-complete compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including features like cross-database queries.
questions.explanation: Managed Instance is specifically designed to closely match on-premises SQL Server behavior, including instance-level features like cross-database queries, which Azure SQL Database does not support in the same way.

questions.question: Azure SQL Database is a platform-as-a-service (PaaS) offering, meaning Microsoft handles operating system and database engine patching.
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database is PaaS, so Microsoft manages the underlying OS and database engine, unlike SQL Server on an Azure VM, which is IaaS and leaves OS management to the customer.

questions.question: Deploying SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine removes all operating system management responsibility from the customer.
questions.explanation: SQL Server on an Azure VM is an IaaS offering, so the customer still manages the operating system themselves; only the underlying physical hardware and virtualization layer are handled by Microsoft.

questions.question: Which of the following are relational database deployment options on Azure? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance are both relational, SQL Server-based deployment options. Azure Cosmos DB and Azure Table Storage are both non-relational (NoSQL) services, not relational databases.

questions.question: An application needs a database that can replicate data across multiple regions worldwide with low-latency reads and writes and configurable consistency levels. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is purpose-built for global distribution with low-latency reads and writes and configurable consistency levels. Azure SQL Database and Table Storage are not designed for turnkey multi-region global distribution in the same way, and Azure Files is a managed file share service, not a globally distributed database.

questions.question: A development team already builds their application using MongoDB drivers and wants to move to a managed Azure database without rewriting their data access code. Which Cosmos DB API fits?
questions.explanation: The API for MongoDB lets an application built against MongoDB drivers connect to Cosmos DB with minimal code changes. The NoSQL (Core) API uses Cosmos DB's native document model instead, the Gremlin API is for graph data, and the Table API is for simple key-value data — none of those preserve existing MongoDB driver code.

questions.question: A company needs to store millions of large video files as objects that applications can retrieve over HTTP, with tiers to reduce cost for rarely accessed files. Which service fits best?
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage is object storage designed for large unstructured files like video, accessible over HTTP, with access tiers to reduce cost for infrequently accessed data. Table Storage holds simple structured key-value entities rather than large binary objects, Azure SQL Database is relational, and Cosmos DB is a broader NoSQL database service, not primarily an object store.

questions.question: A big data analytics workload needs an Azure Blob Storage account organized with real directories and folders, plus fine-grained permissions on those folders, for efficient large-scale analytics. Which capability enables this?
options: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (hierarchical namespace)
questions.explanation: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 adds a hierarchical namespace of real directories and folders with fine-grained permissions on top of Blob Storage, purpose-built for large-scale analytics. The Archive tier and RA-GRS are cost and redundancy settings, not a namespace structure, and Table Storage is an entirely separate, non-hierarchical key-value store.

questions.question: Which of these is the best example of a use case suited to a NoSQL document database rather than a relational database?
options: Enforcing strict referential integrity between financial ledger transactions
Running complex multi-table joins across normalized tables
Guaranteeing full ACID compliance across multiple related tables
Storing product catalog items where each product has a different, evolving set of attributes
questions.explanation: A document database handles a catalog where each product can have a different, evolving set of attributes far more naturally than a rigid relational schema would. Referential integrity, complex joins, and full ACID compliance across related tables are all strengths of relational databases, not typical reasons to choose a NoSQL document store.

questions.question: A company wants to fully replace an aging on-premises file server with a cloud equivalent that can still be mounted using the standard SMB protocol from multiple machines. Which service fits?
questions.explanation: Azure Files provides fully managed file shares accessible over the standard SMB protocol, letting it act as a drop-in replacement for an on-premises file server mounted by multiple machines. Blob Storage and Cosmos DB are not mounted as traditional file shares, and Table Storage holds structured entities, not files.

questions.question: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model database service designed for low-latency access at large scale.
questions.explanation: This is the core description of Cosmos DB — global distribution, multiple data models and APIs, and low-latency access guarantees.

questions.question: Azure Table Storage is the recommended Azure service for storing large binary files such as videos and images.
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage is designed for large unstructured binary files like video and images. Table Storage instead stores simple structured key-value entities, not large binary objects.

questions.question: Which of the following are considered non-relational (NoSQL) Azure data stores? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB, Table Storage, and Blob Storage are all non-relational stores, holding documents, key-value entities, and unstructured objects respectively. Azure SQL Database is a relational, SQL Server-based service, not NoSQL.

questions.question: In a star schema used for a sales data warehouse, which table would store the numeric sales amounts and quantities to be aggregated?
questions.explanation: The fact table in a star schema stores the numeric, measurable values, like sales amounts and quantities, that get aggregated. Dimension tables, like Date, Product, and Customer, store descriptive context used to filter and group those facts, not the measurements themselves.

questions.question: A modern cloud analytics pipeline loads raw data directly into a powerful destination system first, and performs all transformations afterward using that destination's own compute. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first and transforms it there, taking advantage of the destination's own compute power — matching the pattern described. ETL transforms data before loading it, OLTP is a transactional workload type unrelated to pipeline ordering, and a star schema is a data modeling pattern, not a load-order pattern.

questions.question: A retailer needs to detect a spike in checkout errors within seconds of it happening, rather than discovering it in a report the next morning. Which processing approach fits?
options: Batch processing on a nightly schedule
questions.explanation: Streaming, or real-time, processing analyzes each event as it arrives, enabling detection within seconds, which fits a checkout-error spike that must be caught immediately. Batch processing, a weekly ETL job, and a monthly-refreshed OLAP cube all introduce a scheduled delay that would miss an issue happening right now.

questions.question: Which Azure service provides both serverless and dedicated SQL pools for querying data, alongside built-in Apache Spark pools, in a single unified analytics workspace?
questions.explanation: Azure Synapse Analytics combines serverless and dedicated SQL pools with built-in Apache Spark pools in one unified workspace. Data Factory focuses on pipeline orchestration rather than querying, Stream Analytics focuses on real-time event processing, and Cosmos DB is a non-relational database, not a SQL and Spark analytics workspace.

questions.question: Which Azure service is purpose-built for orchestrating and scheduling data movement and transformation pipelines between many different source and destination systems?
questions.explanation: Azure Data Factory is built specifically to orchestrate and schedule data movement and transformation pipelines across many source and destination systems. Power BI visualizes data rather than moving it, Databricks executes big-data processing and machine learning code, and Table Storage is simply a data store, not an orchestration service.

questions.question: A data science team needs an Apache Spark-based environment for large-scale data engineering and machine learning model training. Which Azure service fits best?
questions.explanation: Azure Databricks is an Apache Spark-based platform purpose-built for large-scale data engineering and machine learning. Table Storage and Files are storage services with no processing engine of their own, and Power BI Desktop is a reporting and visualization tool, not a data science or Spark environment.

questions.question: Which Azure service is designed specifically to run continuous SQL-like queries directly against a live stream of IoT telemetry as it arrives?
questions.explanation: Azure Stream Analytics runs continuous, SQL-like queries directly against live streaming data, such as IoT telemetry, as it arrives. Data Factory is built for scheduled batch orchestration rather than continuous stream queries, SQL Managed Instance is a relational database, and Table Storage is a static data store with no streaming query engine.

questions.question: Which platform unifies data engineering, data warehousing, data integration, and Power BI into a single SaaS experience built on one shared data lake called OneLake?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Fabric is the SaaS platform that unifies data engineering, data warehousing, data integration, and Power BI on a single shared data lake, OneLake. Synapse, Databricks, and Data Factory are each strong individual pieces of that broader picture, but none of them alone is the unified, OneLake-based SaaS platform described.

questions.question: A Power BI report needs to always reflect the very latest data in its source database at the moment a user opens it, even if query performance is slightly slower as a result. Which connectivity mode should be used?
options: A scheduled nightly refresh of an imported dataset
Exporting the data to a CSV file first
questions.explanation: DirectQuery leaves data in its source system and queries it live on every interaction, so the report always reflects the latest data, at some performance cost. Import mode copies data into an in-memory model that is only as fresh as its last scheduled refresh, and exporting to CSV first would make the data even more stale, not less.

questions.question: Streaming (real-time) analytics processes data continuously as it arrives, while batch processing handles data in large scheduled groups.
questions.explanation: This is the standard distinction between the two processing models tested on this exam.

questions.question: In a data warehouse star schema, fact tables typically store descriptive attributes, while dimension tables store the numeric measurements.
questions.explanation: This has it backwards: fact tables store the numeric, measurable values to be aggregated, while dimension tables store the descriptive context, like product or customer details, used to filter and group those facts.

questions.question: Azure Data Factory is primarily used for creating Power BI reports rather than orchestrating data pipelines.
questions.explanation: Azure Data Factory is built for orchestrating and scheduling data movement and transformation pipelines, not for authoring reports — that is Power BI's role.

questions.question: Azure Databricks is built on Apache Spark and is commonly used for large-scale data engineering and machine learning workloads.
questions.explanation: Databricks is an Apache Spark-based platform specifically aimed at big-data processing, data engineering, and machine learning at scale.

questions.question: Microsoft Fabric unifies data engineering, data warehousing, data integration, and Power BI into a single SaaS platform built on OneLake.
questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic of Microsoft Fabric — one SaaS platform spanning these workloads, backed by a single shared data lake called OneLake.

questions.question: Which of the following are capabilities provided within Azure Synapse Analytics? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Synapse Analytics provides serverless SQL pools, dedicated SQL pools, and built-in Apache Spark pools within one workspace. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a separate identity service unrelated to Synapse's analytics capabilities.

questions.question: Which data professional role is primarily responsible for building, training, and evaluating machine learning models from data, as distinct from maintaining the database itself or building descriptive dashboards?
questions.explanation: A Data Scientist builds, trains, and evaluates predictive machine learning models from data. A Database Administrator focuses on provisioning and maintaining databases, a Business Analyst focuses on business requirements rather than model building, and a Data Analyst builds descriptive reports and visualizations rather than predictive models.

questions.question: A relational database enforces a rule that an account balance can never go negative, and rejects any transaction that would violate this rule, always leaving the database in a valid state. Which ACID property does this describe?
questions.explanation: Consistency guarantees that a transaction only ever moves the database from one valid state to another, enforcing rules like a balance constraint and rejecting anything that would violate it. Atomicity is about a transaction being all-or-nothing, Durability is about committed changes surviving a crash, and Isolation is about concurrent transactions not interfering with each other — none of which describe enforcing a specific business rule like this one.

questions.question: A relational database table has a frequently searched column with no index. What is the primary benefit of adding an index on that column?
options: It encrypts the column's data at rest
It enforces that the column's values are unique
It automatically normalizes the surrounding table structure
It speeds up read queries by avoiding a full table scan
questions.explanation: An index lets the database engine locate matching rows quickly instead of scanning every row in the table, speeding up read queries. Indexes do not encrypt data, and while a unique index can enforce uniqueness, that is a separate, optional constraint rather than an index's primary general-purpose benefit, and indexing has nothing to do with normalizing a table's structure.

questions.question: A company runs 50 small Azure SQL databases with unpredictable usage that rarely peaks for every database at the same time. Provisioning each database for its own worst case would be expensive. Which deployment option lets these databases share a pool of resources to reduce cost?
options: An elastic pool sharing resources across many databases
SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine
A single database sized for its own peak load
questions.explanation: An elastic pool lets many databases with staggered, non-simultaneous usage share one billed pool of resources instead of each being sized for its own peak, matching this cost-saving scenario. SQL Server on a VM adds unrelated OS management overhead, sizing every database for its own peak is the expensive approach being avoided, and read scale-out only offloads read queries to a replica rather than pooling resources across many databases.

questions.question: In Azure Cosmos DB, what unit is the throughput a container consumes measured and billed in?
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB throughput is provisioned and billed in Request Units per second (RU/s), a currency representing the cost of database operations. DTUs and vCores are purchasing units for Azure SQL Database instead, and generic IOPS is not the unit Cosmos DB uses to measure or bill throughput.

questions.question: A company needs to run fast, ad hoc analytical queries over huge volumes of time-stamped log and telemetry data, using a Kusto Query Language (KQL)-based service. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
questions.explanation: Azure Data Explorer is purpose-built for fast, ad hoc exploration of huge volumes of log and telemetry data using KQL. Azure Data Factory orchestrates data movement and transformation rather than running ad hoc analytical queries itself, and Table Storage and Azure Database for MySQL are general-purpose data stores with no built-in large-scale log analytics query engine.

questions.question: In Power BI, which artifact is a collection of visualizations pinned together from one or more reports into a single, consolidated view, often used for at-a-glance monitoring?
questions.explanation: A dashboard is a single-page collection of visualizations, or tiles, pinned from one or more reports for at-a-glance monitoring. A dataset is the underlying data model a report queries, a dataflow is a reusable, prepared set of data built with Power Query, and a workspace is a container that organizes datasets, reports, and dashboards together rather than being a visualization itself.

questions.question: A data lake requires data to already be structured and modeled with a fixed schema before it can be ingested, similar to a data warehouse.
questions.explanation: A data lake is designed to accept raw data of any type or structure without requiring a schema up front, unlike a data warehouse, which expects data to already be structured and modeled before it arrives.

questions.question: Azure SQL Database provides built-in high availability without requiring the customer to manually configure and manage a separate failover cluster.
questions.explanation: High availability is built into Azure SQL Database automatically as part of the managed PaaS service, with no customer-configured failover cluster required, unlike a self-managed SQL Server deployment on a virtual machine.

questions.question: An Azure Synapse serverless SQL pool bills based on the volume of data processed by each query, rather than for pre-allocated, always-on compute resources.
questions.explanation: Serverless SQL pools use a pay-per-query, consumption-based billing model tied to the data processed by each query, rather than charging for continuously provisioned compute the way a dedicated SQL pool does.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about Azure Blob Storage access tiers? (Select all that apply)
options: Archive tier offers the lowest storage cost but requires rehydration before data can be read
Hot tier is intended for frequently accessed data
Cool tier has a lower storage cost than Hot but higher access costs
All access tiers require the same minimum retention period
questions.explanation: Archive offers the lowest storage cost but needs rehydration before reading, Hot is meant for frequently accessed data at the lowest access cost, and Cool trades a lower storage cost for higher per-access cost than Hot. Access tiers do not all share the same minimum retention period — Cool and Cold generally carry longer minimum retention requirements than Hot, and Archive's is longer still.

questions.question: Which of the following are core components of Microsoft Fabric? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Microsoft Fabric unifies OneLake as its single shared data lake, Power BI for reporting, and Data Factory-style pipelines for data integration, all in one SaaS platform. Windows Admin Center is an unrelated on-premises Windows Server management tool with no connection to Microsoft Fabric.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: You have 45 minutes for 50 questions — about 0.9 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 75%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you get partial credit for nothing by running out of time on one question.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Relational vs. non-relational
points: Relational = fixed schema, tables with rows/columns, relationships enforced by foreign keys, queried with SQL, strong for structured data and ACID transactions.
Non-relational (NoSQL) trades a fixed schema for flexibility and horizontal scale — it comes in four flavors: document, key-value, column-family, and graph.

Document store (JSON-like documents, e.g. Cosmos DB NoSQL/MongoDB APIs) vs. key-value (fast lookup by key, e.g. Table Storage/Redis) vs. column-family (wide, sparse columns, e.g. Cassandra API) vs. graph (nodes + edges for relationships, e.g. Gremlin API).
Normalization (splitting data across related tables to reduce redundancy) is a relational concept; NoSQL stores often intentionally denormalize for read speed.

cheatSheet.heading: OLTP vs. OLAP
points: OLTP = many short, frequent read/write transactions (e.g. order entry) — normalized schema, optimized for speed and consistency.
OLAP = complex analytical queries over large historical volumes — typically denormalized into a star schema, optimized for aggregation and reporting.
Star schema = a central fact table (numeric measures) surrounded by dimension tables (descriptive attributes like date, product, customer).
Azure SQL Database is a classic OLTP engine; Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools are built for OLAP-style analytics.

cheatSheet.heading: Core Azure relational services
points: Azure SQL Database = fully managed PaaS, single/pooled databases, least management overhead, least SQL Server surface-area compatibility of the three.
Azure SQL Managed Instance = near-100% SQL Server engine compatibility with PaaS management — the middle ground for lift-and-shift with minimal code changes.
SQL Server on Azure VM = IaaS, full control and full compatibility, but you patch/manage the OS and SQL Server yourself.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL = managed open-source relational engines for non-SQL Server workloads.

cheatSheet.heading: Core Azure non-relational & analytics services
points: Cosmos DB = globally distributed, multi-model (via APIs), single-digit-millisecond latency, with five tunable consistency levels from Strong to Eventual.
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 = hierarchical namespace on top of Blob storage, built for large-scale big-data analytics, not a database engine itself.
Azure Synapse Analytics unifies data warehousing (dedicated SQL pools) and big-data processing (serverless SQL pools, Spark pools) in one service.
Azure Data Factory orchestrates ETL/ELT pipelines to move and transform data — it does not store data itself.
Azure Databricks = an Apache Spark-based analytics platform for big-data processing and machine learning, notebook-driven.
Microsoft Fabric unifies OneLake (one shared data lake), Power BI, and Data Factory-style pipelines into a single SaaS analytics platform.

cheatSheet.heading: Batch vs. streaming, and data shapes
points: Batch processing = large volumes processed on a schedule (e.g. nightly ETL); streaming = near real-time processing as data arrives (e.g. Azure Stream Analytics, Event Hubs).
Structured data = strict tabular schema (rows/columns). Semi-structured = flexible but self-describing (JSON, XML). Unstructured = no inherent schema (images, video, free text).
A data warehouse stores curated, structured/modeled data for reporting; a data lake stores raw data of any shape at scale, structure applied later (schema-on-read).

cheatSheet.heading: Data professional roles
points: Database Administrator (DBA) — designs, secures, monitors, and maintains database systems day to day.
Data Engineer — builds and manages the pipelines and infrastructure that move and transform data for analytics.
Data Analyst — explores data and builds reports/dashboards to drive business decisions, commonly using Power BI.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: DP-900 is knowledge-level and vendor-neutral in spots — expect "which service is best suited for X" questions rather than deep hands-on configuration.
When a question mentions relationships between entities that matter as much as the entities themselves, that's pointing at a graph database, not a document store.
"All access tiers share the same minimum retention period" is a common false-answer trap — Cool/Cold/Archive carry longer minimum retention than Hot.
If the scenario says "structure isn't known until read time," that's schema-on-read (data lake), not schema-on-write (relational database).
